title: Market Failure and the Role of Government

guide.summary: Unit 6 examines when markets fail to allocate resources efficiently and how government can respond: externalities and corrective taxes and subsidies, public goods and the free-rider problem, government interventions in different market structures (including antitrust), and income inequality and tax systems.

sections.heading: Efficiency and externalities
sections.body: A market is socially efficient where marginal social benefit (MSB) equals marginal social cost (MSC). An externality is a cost or benefit to third parties. Negative externalities (pollution): MSC = MPC + external cost lies above MPC, so the market overproduces (Q_market > Q_socially optimal) and charges too low a price; deadweight loss is the triangle between the two quantities, bounded by MSC and MSB. A Pigouvian (per-unit) tax equal to the marginal external cost shifts MPC up to MSC and corrects the overproduction. Positive externalities (vaccines, education): MSB = MPB + external benefit lies above MPB, so the market underproduces; a per-unit subsidy equal to the marginal external benefit corrects it. Other tools: regulation, tradable permits (cap and trade), and Coase bargaining when transaction costs are low and property rights are clear.

sections.heading: Public goods
sections.body: Goods are classified by rivalry and excludability. Private goods: rival and excludable. Public goods: nonrival (one person's use doesn't reduce another's) and nonexcludable (people can't be prevented from using them), such as national defense and lighthouses. Common resources: rival but nonexcludable (fish in the ocean), prone to overuse. Club goods: nonrival but excludable (streaming services). Because people can benefit without paying (free-rider problem), markets underprovide public goods, so they are often provided by government and funded by taxes.

sections.heading: Government in different market structures
sections.body: Antitrust policy prevents monopolies from forming through mergers and prohibits collusion. Price regulation of natural monopolies can raise output toward the efficient level. A per-unit tax reduces output in any market structure; a lump-sum tax on a monopolist reduces profit without changing output. Price ceilings on a monopolist can increase output. Government interventions can also create inefficiencies (government failure).

sections.heading: Inequality
sections.body: The Lorenz curve plots the cumulative share of income against the cumulative share of households; the farther it bows from the line of perfect equality, the greater the inequality. The Gini coefficient ranges from 0 (perfect equality) to 1 (one household has all income). Sources of inequality include differences in human capital, discrimination, inheritance, and market power. Taxes: progressive (higher-income households pay a larger percentage of income, like the U.S. federal income tax), proportional (same percentage), regressive (lower-income households pay a larger percentage, like sales taxes in effect). Transfer payments and progressive taxes reduce inequality.

sections.heading: Worked example: externalities
sections.body: When producing a good creates pollution, the marginal social cost exceeds the marginal private cost, so the market overproduces the good and charges too low a price. A per-unit tax equal to the marginal external cost shifts private cost up to social cost, moving output to the socially optimal quantity and eliminating deadweight loss. When a good creates positive externalities, such as vaccinations, the marginal social benefit exceeds the marginal private benefit, the market underproduces, and a per-unit subsidy to buyers or sellers can correct it.

sections.heading: Public goods and inequality
sections.body: Public goods are nonrival and nonexcludable, so the free-rider problem leads markets to underprovide them; governments often provide national defense and public parks. Inequality is measured with the Lorenz curve and the Gini coefficient, which ranges from 0 (perfect equality) to 1 (perfect inequality). Progressive taxes take a larger percentage from higher incomes, while regressive taxes take a larger percentage from lower incomes.

sections.heading: Graph checklist
sections.body: For a negative externality, draw demand (MPB), supply (MPC), and a higher MSC curve. Mark the market quantity where MPB = MPC and the socially optimal quantity where MPB = MSC. Shade the deadweight loss triangle between the two quantities, bounded by MSC and MPB. For a positive externality, draw MSB above MPB and shade the triangle at underproduction.

sections.heading: Key terms
sections.body: Know allocative efficiency, marginal social benefit and cost, Pigouvian tax, free rider, public good, common resource, Lorenz curve, Gini coefficient, and progressive and regressive taxes. The tragedy of the commons describes overuse of rival but nonexcludable resources such as fisheries.

keyTakeaways: Public goods: nonrival + nonexcludable → free riders.
Lorenz curve farther from equality line = more inequality.
Progressive taxes take a larger percentage from higher incomes.
commonMistakes: Placing DWL on the wrong side of the socially optimal quantity.
Calling a good public just because government provides it.
Defining regressive tax by the dollar amount instead of the percentage of income.
Saying a Pigouvian tax eliminates pollution entirely (it brings output to the efficient level).
examTips: Externality graphs: label MPC, MSC (or MPB, MSB), Q_market, Q_optimal, and the DWL triangle.
State the size of the corrective tax or subsidy: equal to the marginal external cost or benefit.
Classify goods with a 2×2 grid of rivalry and excludability.
For tax-type questions, compute tax ÷ income for each household.
guide.cramSheet:
**Efficiency:** MSB = MSC

**Negative ext:** MSC > MPC · Q_market > Q_opt · tax = MEC

**Positive ext:** MSB > MPB · Q_market < Q_opt · subsidy = MEB

**DWL:** triangle between Q_market and Q_opt

**Goods:** private (R, E) · public (NR, NE) · common (R, NE) · club (NR, E) · free riders

**Antitrust:** block mergers, ban collusion

**Inequality:** Lorenz · Gini 0–1 · progressive / proportional / regressive (by % of income)

practice.stem: A factory's pollution harms downstream fishers. Without government intervention, the market for the factory's product will

choices.text: produce less than the socially optimal quantity
produce more than the socially optimal quantity

practice.explanation: The factory ignores external costs, so private cost is below social cost.

practice.stem: Which is the best example of a public good?
practice.explanation: National defense is nonrival and nonexcludable.

practice.stem: A tax takes $2,000 from a household earning $20,000 and $5,000 from a household earning $100,000. This tax is
practice.explanation: 10% of the lower income vs. 5% of the higher income.

distractors.A: Judges by dollar amount instead of percentage.

practice.stem: Which policy would best correct the underconsumption of flu vaccines?

choices.text: A per-unit subsidy for vaccines equal to the marginal external benefit

practice.explanation: Vaccines have positive externalities; a subsidy raises quantity to the efficient level.

practice.stem: On a graph of a market with a negative production externality, the deadweight loss is the area

choices.text: between MPC and MSC from zero to the optimal quantity
below the demand curve and above the price
between MSC and demand from the socially optimal quantity to the market quantity
to the left of the socially optimal quantity

practice.explanation: Units beyond the optimum cost society more than they're worth to buyers.

practice.stem: Why do private markets typically underprovide fireworks displays over a city?

choices.text: Because people who don't pay can still watch, so private firms can't collect enough revenue: the free-rider problem.
Because demand for fireworks is perfectly elastic.

practice.stem: Country A's Lorenz curve lies farther from the line of perfect equality than Country B's. Which is true?

choices.text: Country A has greater income inequality and a higher Gini coefficient.
Both have the same Gini coefficient.
Country A has higher average income.

practice.explanation: A larger gap between the curve and the equality line means more inequality.

distractors.D: Lorenz curves show distribution, not levels.

practice.topic: 6.4 The Effects of Government Intervention in Different Market Structures
practice.stem: Two large airlines propose a merger that would give them 70% of flights on many routes. The government blocks the merger. This is an example of
practice.explanation: Antitrust laws prevent mergers that would substantially reduce competition.

practice.stem: A per-unit tax equal to the marginal external cost is placed on a polluting good. Which outcome results?

choices.text: Output falls to the socially optimal level and deadweight loss is eliminated.

practice.explanation: The tax internalizes the external cost: MPC + tax = MSC.

practice.stem: Fish in an unregulated international fishing ground are best classified as

choices.text: a common resource, likely to be overused

practice.explanation: Rival (a fish caught by one isn't available to another) but nonexcludable.

practice.stimulus: In a market, MPB = 100 − Q and MPC = 20 + Q. Each unit produced creates $20 of external cost.
practice.stem: What are the market quantity, socially optimal quantity, and deadweight loss?
A government issues a fixed number of tradable pollution permits to firms. Compared with requiring every firm to cut pollution by the same amount, this approach

choices.text: achieves the same total reduction at lower total cost, because firms with low abatement costs cut more and sell permits
raises the total cost of reducing pollution

practice.explanation: Trading lets abatement happen where it's cheapest.

practice.topic: 6.4 The Effects of Government Intervention in Different Market Structures
practice.stem: A government sets a price ceiling on an unregulated monopolist at the price where MC intersects demand. Which result is most likely?

choices.text: Output increases to the allocatively efficient level and deadweight loss falls.
A shortage develops as in a competitive market.

practice.explanation: With a ceiling, MR equals the ceiling price up to the demand curve, so the monopolist produces where P = MC.

practice.topic: 6.1 Socially Efficient and Inefficient Market Outcomes
practice.stem: Under what condition would private bargaining between a polluting factory and nearby residents most likely reach the efficient outcome without government intervention?

choices.text: Many thousands of residents are affected.
Property rights are clearly defined and transaction costs are low.
The pollution affects only future generations.

practice.explanation: This is the Coase theorem; large numbers and high transaction costs prevent bargaining.

practice.prompt: The production of fertilizer generates water pollution that harms people living downstream. The fertilizer market is perfectly competitive.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Draw (describe) a correctly labeled graph of the fertilizer market showing the demand (MPB = MSB), MPC, and MSC curves. Label the market quantity Q_m and the socially optimal quantity Q_s.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Identify a per-unit government policy that would move output to Q_s, and state its size.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Explain why the policy in (c) does not reduce pollution to zero.

rubric.description: Axes price and quantity; demand (MPB = MSB); MPC; MSC above MPC.
Q_m where MPC meets demand; Q_s where MSC meets demand; Q_s < Q_m.
Triangle between Q_s and Q_m, bounded above by MSC and below by demand.
A per-unit (Pigouvian) tax equal to the marginal external cost (vertical distance between MSC and MPC).
At Q_s, the benefit of the last unit of fertilizer equals its full social cost, including pollution; eliminating all pollution would forgo units whose benefits exceed their social costs.

practice.sampleResponse:
(a) The graph has 'Price' on the vertical axis and 'Quantity of fertilizer' on the horizontal axis. A downward-sloping demand curve is labeled MPB = MSB. An upward-sloping MPC curve intersects demand at Q_m. An MSC curve lies above MPC by the marginal external cost and intersects demand at Q_s, to the left of Q_m.

(b) Deadweight loss is the triangle between Q_s and Q_m, bounded above by MSC and below by the demand curve.

(c) A per-unit tax on fertilizer equal to the marginal external cost of the pollution, which is the vertical distance between MSC and MPC.

(d) The tax reduces output to Q_s, where the marginal social benefit of fertilizer equals its marginal social cost including pollution. Cutting output below Q_s to eliminate all pollution would give up fertilizer whose value to society exceeds its full cost, so some pollution is efficient.
